task-intent.statement: Resume a frozen gate plan (execute.json) after the issue it plans was re-scoped mid-run by the human, and drive it to a terminal spine.

expected-behavior.statement: The frozen gates' acceptance checks would either still hold under the new scope or fail visibly in a way that named what had changed.

observed-behavior.statement: Two of the frozen checks were wrong, in OPPOSITE directions, and neither would have announced why. g4's c1 (checks/dispositions_done.py) required EXACTLY ONE surviving active lesson and failed on zero -- correct under the withdrawn scope where disposing that one lesson was the pending decision, and the exact inverse of the new requirement, where zero is the target. g5's c2 was a bash-negated grep for 'agent-work/LESSONS.md' over skills/commander/templates/COMMANDER_SPINE.template.json; that file holds SIX occurrences and only two are the read path the gate was cutting -- the other four are the lessons writer, which the same gate's own constraints require survive -- so the check was satisfiable only by destroying what the gate existed to preserve. Both were corrected through the engine's amend verb (rescope and retext-check) rather than waived, and both replacements were verified RED before the work that would make them green.

impact-cost.statement: No rework: both were found by reading the checks against the re-scope before starting their gates, so neither ever blocked or falsely passed. Cost was two amend deltas. Had either been waived instead of corrected, the run would have finished green with a check in the tree asserting the opposite of its requirement.

workaround.statement: Correct the check through the engine's sanctioned re-planning verbs (amend rescope for a gate, amend retext-check for one condition) rather than waiving it, and re-verify the replacement RED before doing the work that turns it green. A waived check stays in the tree asserting the old rule; a corrected one becomes the acceptance test the gate actually needs.

task-intent.statement: Author the g5 implementer handoff, enumerating which occurrences of .agent-work/LESSONS.md in skills/commander/templates/COMMANDER_SPINE.template.json must be removed and which must survive, so the crew could not destroy the writer while cutting the read path.

expected-behavior.statement: The count stated in the handoff -- five occurrences, two removed and three surviving -- would match the file.

observed-behavior.statement: The file holds SIX occurrences, four of which survive: the feedback imperative invokes apply_lessons_delta.py twice, and the handoff counted that as one. This is the THIRD instance of an under-inclusive enumeration presented as complete within issue #308 alone -- see episode issue-308-021, which records the first two, both committed by this run's predecessor while planning the consolidation of that same failure mode. It was caught by the g5 reviewer following an instruction the same handoff carried: verify the surviving writer BY CONTENT, not by count. That instruction is the rule of episode issue-308-002 (verify a claim against the code before using it as a premise), applied by a crew against the agent that had just migrated it.

impact-cost.statement: No rework and no defect shipped: the implementer's own pre-edit measurement showed the writer lines matched none of the guard's markers, so the gate was satisfiable by cutting exactly the two read-path sites with no pressure toward the writer, and the reviewer's by-content check confirmed all four survivors afterwards. Recurrence count for this pattern within one issue: 3, by two different agents. The cost was zero because the counter-measure fired, not because the enumeration was right.

workaround.statement: Instruct the downstream reader to verify BY CONTENT rather than by count, naming each item that must survive, so a wrong total in the handoff cannot become a wrong action. The count was wrong and the work was still correct, because nothing depended on the count alone.
